stem: A 68-year-old man has sudden hoarseness, trouble swallowing and dizziness. Pinprick and cold are lost on the right side of his face and the left side of his arm, leg and trunk. The right vocal cord is paralyzed and the right gag reflex is absent. Strength is normal.
oneliner: 68M + sudden hoarseness, dysphagia, dizziness, right face and left body pain/temperature loss, right cord palsy, strength normal → where is the lesion?

whyNot.A: A **left** lesion would take the **left** face and **right** body; his **face loss is on the right**
whyNot.B: The ventromedial medulla holds the pyramid and hypoglossal root, which cause **weakness**; his **strength is normal**
whyNot.D: The pons does not hold the nucleus ambiguus, so it would not explain **hoarseness and an absent gag**
whyNot.E: The midbrain would cause **eye movement** problems, not **vocal cord paralysis and absent gag**

answer: Right dorsolateral (lateral) medulla (lateral medullary syndrome; PICA or vertebral artery)
why: **Same-side face** and **opposite-side body** loss of pain and temperature (spinal trigeminal nucleus and spinothalamic tract) with **hoarseness and absent gag** (nucleus ambiguus) is the **lateral medullary syndrome**. The lesion is on the side of the **facial** loss, the **right**, and the posterior inferior cerebellar or vertebral artery is the usual culprit.

idea.rule: Crossed findings (face on one side, body on the other) with bulbar signs place the lesion in the lateral medulla on the face side.
also: Nucleus ambiguus damage: hoarseness, dysphagia, absent gag
Spinal trigeminal nucleus: ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss
Spinothalamic fibers have already crossed: contralateral body loss
Vestibular nuclei involvement adds vertigo and nystagmus

stem: A 70-year-old man has sudden weakness of the left arm and leg. When he sticks out his tongue it points to the right. Facial sensation, voice and swallowing are normal.
oneliner: 70M + sudden left arm and leg weakness, tongue deviates right, face sensation, voice, swallowing normal → where is the lesion?

options.D: Left posterior limb of the internal capsule

whyNot.A: The lateral medulla causes **crossed sensory loss and hoarseness**; his **sensation and voice are normal** and he has **weakness**
whyNot.B: A **pontine** lesion would leave the tongue turning **left**, toward the weak side, not **right**
whyNot.C: A peduncle lesion would likewise turn the tongue to the **left**; his **tongue goes right**, to the lesion side
whyNot.D: A **left** capsule lesion would weaken the **right** limbs; his weakness is on the **left**

answer: Right medial medulla (pyramid and hypoglossal root; anterior spinal artery)
why: **Opposite-side limb weakness** with **same-side tongue weakness** (the tongue turns toward the weak side, here the right) places the lesion in the **medial medulla**: the pyramid before it crosses and the exiting **hypoglossal** fibers. The anterior spinal artery supplies it.

idea.rule: Medial medullary lesions: opposite limb weakness with same-side tongue deviation.
also: Hypoglossal nerve lesions turn the tongue toward the injured side
Corticospinal fibers cross at the caudal medulla
The anterior spinal artery supplies the medullary pyramids
Lateral medullary syndrome is PICA and spares the tongue
Medial lemniscus damage adds opposite-side loss of vibration and position sense

stem: A 53-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes has sudden double vision. The right eyelid droops. The right eye sits down and out and cannot adduct or move vertically, and the right pupil is large and does not react to light.
oneliner: 53F + HTN, diabetes, sudden diplopia, right ptosis, eye down and out, dilated fixed right pupil → which additional deficit?
ask: Which additional finding is most likely?

options.A: Weakness of the left arm and leg
options.B: Weakness of the right arm and leg
options.C: Complete paralysis of the right face
options.D: Deviation of the tongue to the right
options.E: Hearing loss in the right ear

whyNot.B: The right peduncle serves the **left** body, so **right**-sided weakness is the wrong side
whyNot.C: Facial nerve palsy points to the **pons**; every sign she has is **third nerve** or midbrain
whyNot.D: Tongue deviation comes from **hypoglossal** damage in the **medulla**; every sign she has is **third nerve** or midbrain
whyNot.E: Hearing loss points to **CN VIII** at the pontomedullary junction or inner ear, not her **third nerve** findings

answer: Left hemiparesis (Weber syndrome: right oculomotor palsy with contralateral weakness)
why: A full **third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil** from a stroke places the lesion in the **ventral midbrain**, where the oculomotor fascicles cross the **cerebral peduncle**. The corticospinal fibers there have not yet crossed, so the weakness is on the **opposite (left)** side; paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery supply the area.

idea.rule: Third nerve palsy plus opposite hemiparesis means ventral midbrain (Weber syndrome).
also: Weber syndrome: ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis
Posterior cerebral artery paramedian branches supply the midbrain
Claude syndrome: CN III palsy with contralateral ataxia (red nucleus)
Benedikt syndrome: CN III palsy with contralateral tremor

stem: A 57-year-old man has had hoarseness and trouble swallowing for 2 days. When he says "ah", the right side of his soft palate does not rise and the uvula is pulled to the left. His eye movements, chewing, facial movement and hearing are normal.
oneliner: 57M + 2 days hoarseness, dysphagia, right palate fails to rise, uvula to left, eyes/chewing/face/hearing normal → where does the damaged nerve leave the brainstem?
ask: At which level does the injured nerve leave the brainstem?

whyNot.A: The midbrain gives off CN III and IV, and his **eye movements are normal**
whyNot.B: The pons gives off **CN V**, and his **chewing is normal**
whyNot.C: The pontomedullary junction gives off VI, VII and VIII, and his **eye movements, facial movement and hearing are normal**
whyNot.E: The cerebellopontine angle holds VII and VIII roots, and his **hearing and facial movement are normal**

why: Hoarseness, dysphagia and a palate that fails to rise on one side mean a **vagus nerve** injury, and the vagus (like IX, XI and XII) leaves the brainstem at the **medulla**. The uvula points **away** from the weak side.

idea.rule: Nerves leave in order: III-IV midbrain, V-VIII pons, IX-XII medulla.
also: CN III and IV exit from the midbrain
CN V exits from the pons; VI, VII, VIII exit at the pontomedullary junction
CN IX, X, XI and XII exit from the medulla
CN IV is the only nerve to exit from the dorsal brainstem

stem: A 65-year-old woman with a known aneurysm of the internal carotid artery inside the cavernous sinus develops double vision when she looks sideways. The eye on the aneurysm side cannot turn outward. Her eyelids and pupils look normal, and vision and facial sensation are normal.
oneliner: 65F + intracavernous carotid aneurysm + horizontal diplopia, eye cannot abduct, lids, pupils, vision, face sensation normal → which nerve is hit first?
ask: Which nerve is most likely injured first?

options.D: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve

whyNot.A: A third nerve palsy would add **ptosis and a dilated pupil**; her **lids and pupils are normal**
whyNot.C: A fourth nerve palsy gives **vertical** diplopia worst looking down and in, but hers is **horizontal**
whyNot.D: V1 damage would numb the **forehead and cornea**; her **facial sensation is normal**
whyNot.E: The optic nerve does not run in the sinus, and her **vision is normal**

why: In the cavernous sinus, CN III, IV, V1 and V2 sit in the **lateral wall**, but the **abducens runs free beside the internal carotid artery**, so an aneurysm presses on it first. The eye cannot **abduct**.

idea.rule: In the cavernous sinus only CN VI lies free beside the carotid, so it fails first.
also: CN III, IV, V1 and V2 lie in the lateral wall of the sinus
Cavernous sinus thrombosis often starts with CN VI palsy
Horner syndrome with CN VI palsy points to the cavernous sinus
The internal carotid artery passes through the sinus

stem: A 55-year-old man with a known tumor at the apex of the left lung has a drooping left eyelid, a small left pupil, and less flushing and sweating of the left face. He is also hoarse.
oneliner: 55M + left apical lung tumor, left ptosis, miosis, less left facial sweating, hoarse → where do the cell bodies of the compressed sympathetic fibers lie?
ask: Where do the cell bodies of the sympathetic neurons compressed at the lung apex lie?

options.A: Superior cervical ganglion in the neck
options.C: Ventral horn of the cord at C8
options.D: Dorsal root ganglion at the T1 level

whyNot.A: The superior cervical ganglion holds **postganglionic** cell bodies; fibers crossing the **lung apex** are still **preganglionic**, on their way up to it
whyNot.B: The Edinger-Westphal nucleus drives pupil **constriction**; its loss makes a **large** pupil, not his **small** one
whyNot.C: The ventral horn holds **somatic motor** neurons; his signs (**ptosis, small pupil, lost sweating**) are **autonomic**
whyNot.D: A dorsal root ganglion holds **sensory** cell bodies; his deficit is **autonomic**

answer: Intermediolateral cell column of the upper thoracic cord (C8-T2)
why: Ptosis, miosis and **loss of facial sweating** are **Horner syndrome**. Lost sweating means the lesion lies **before the superior cervical ganglion**, on the **preganglionic** neurons that pass over the lung apex. Their cell bodies are in the **intermediolateral cell column (C8-T2)**.

idea.rule: Preganglionic oculosympathetic neurons arise in the lateral horn (intermediolateral column) at C8-T2.
also: Pancoast tumor causes Horner syndrome and shoulder or arm pain
First-order neurons start in the hypothalamus
Second-order neurons leave the cord and pass over the lung apex
Third-order neurons from the superior cervical ganglion travel with the carotid

stem: A 62-year-old right-handed man with atrial fibrillation has sudden trouble speaking. He talks in effortful phrases of three or four words but follows commands normally. The lower right side of his face droops.
oneliner: 62M right-handed + AF, sudden effortful 3-4 word speech, comprehension normal, right lower face droop → which cortical area?

whyNot.A: The left posterior superior temporal gyrus causes **fluent** speech with **poor comprehension**; he **understands** commands
whyNot.B: An arcuate lesion causes poor **repetition** with **fluent** speech; his speech is **effortful and nonfluent**
whyNot.D: The angular gyrus causes **reading and writing** problems with fluent speech, not **halting speech**
whyNot.E: In a **right-handed** man language sits on the **left**, and a right-sided area does not explain **right face weakness**

answer: Left posterior inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area)
why: Effortful, short-phrase speech with **intact comprehension** is **Broca aphasia**. The lesion is in the **left posterior inferior frontal gyrus**, which lies beside the face motor cortex and explains the **right lower face weakness**; the superior division of the left MCA supplies it, and an embolus from atrial fibrillation fits.

idea.rule: Nonfluent speech with intact comprehension is Broca area; it sits next to the face motor cortex.
also: Broca aphasia: nonfluent, comprehension intact, repetition poor
Patients are aware of their errors and are often frustrated
Superior division of the left MCA supplies the frontal language area
Right-sided face and arm weakness often accompany it

stem: A 68-year-old right-handed man has a sudden stroke. He talks fluently in long sentences, but the words are wrong or invented, he cannot follow spoken commands or repeat a phrase, and he seems unaware of the errors. His limb strength is normal.
oneliner: 68M right-handed + sudden fluent nonsense speech, cannot follow commands or repeat, unaware, strength normal → which cortical area?

whyNot.B: A lesion of the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus would make speech **effortful**, but his is **fluent**
whyNot.C: An arcuate lesion leaves **comprehension intact**; he **cannot follow commands**
whyNot.D: A supplementary motor area lesion **cuts speech output** but spares **repetition**; his speech is **abundant** and he **cannot repeat**
whyNot.E: In a **right-handed** man language lives in the **left** hemisphere, not the right

answer: Left posterior superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke area)
why: Fluent speech full of wrong and made-up words, **poor comprehension** and **poor repetition**, with no weakness, is **Wernicke aphasia**. The lesion is in the **left posterior superior temporal gyrus**, supplied by the inferior division of the left MCA.

idea.rule: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension is Wernicke area.
also: Wernicke aphasia: fluent, comprehension poor, repetition poor
Inferior division of the left MCA supplies the temporal language area
Patients are usually unaware of their errors
A superior quadrantanopia can accompany temporal lesions

stem: A 74-year-old man has a stroke on the left side of the brain. He speaks fluently and understands what is said, but he cannot repeat a phrase the examiner says and makes sound errors when naming objects.
oneliner: 74M + left hemisphere stroke, fluent speech, comprehension normal, cannot repeat, naming errors → which structure?

whyNot.A: The uncinate fasciculus links the temporal pole with the orbitofrontal cortex and is not the **repetition pathway** between language areas
whyNot.B: A supplementary motor area lesion **cuts speech output** and spares **repetition**; his speech is **fluent** and **repetition fails**
whyNot.C: A lesion of the left posterior superior temporal gyrus would give **poor comprehension**; he **understands** well
whyNot.E: A lesion of the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus would make speech **nonfluent**; his is **fluent**

why: **Fluent** speech and **normal comprehension** with **poor repetition** is **conduction aphasia**. The lesion cuts the **arcuate fasciculus**, the tract linking the Wernicke and Broca areas.

idea.rule: Isolated poor repetition with fluent speech and good comprehension is a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus.
also: Conduction aphasia: fluent, comprehension intact, repetition poor
The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke and Broca areas
Patients know they are wrong and try to correct themselves
Transcortical aphasias spare repetition

stem: A 65-year-old woman has gone deaf in both ears over many years from loss of her cochlear hair cells, and hearing aids no longer help. A cochlear implant is placed, with an array of electrodes inside the cochlea, and she begins to hear sounds.
oneliner: 65F + severe bilateral sensorineural deafness from hair cell loss + implant electrodes in the cochlea → what do they stimulate?
ask: Which structure do the electrodes stimulate directly?

options.A: Inner hair cells of the organ of Corti
options.B: Auditory nerve endings in the cochlea
options.C: Ossicular chain of the middle ear
options.D: Round window membrane at the base
options.E: Cochlear nuclei in the lower brainstem

whyNot.A: Her **hair cells are lost**, so stimulating them would do nothing
whyNot.C: The ossicles carry sound in the **middle ear**; the implant sits in the **cochlea**, past them
whyNot.D: The round window membrane only relieves pressure; the electrodes act on **neural tissue** inside the cochlea
whyNot.E: The cochlear nuclei lie in the **brainstem**, beyond the cochlear electrodes (a brainstem implant is a different device)

answer: Auditory (spiral ganglion) nerve fibers in the cochlea
why: The implant **bypasses the lost hair cells** and fires electrodes next to **spiral ganglion fibers of the auditory nerve**. It therefore needs an **intact cochlear nerve**.

idea.rule: A cochlear implant skips the hair cells and stimulates the auditory nerve, so the nerve must be intact.
also: Sensorineural loss from hair cell damage suits an implant
An absent cochlear nerve calls for an auditory brainstem implant
Hearing aids amplify sound and need some surviving hair cells
The spiral ganglion holds the cell bodies of auditory nerve fibers

stem: A 16-year-old boy dives into a shallow pool and injures his neck. He now has a stiff, weak right arm and leg with brisk reflexes and an upgoing right toe. Pain and temperature sensation are normal on both sides.
oneliner: 16M + shallow dive neck injury, stiff weak right arm and leg, brisk reflexes, right Babinski, pain/temperature normal → which tract?
ask: Which side and tract is damaged?

whyNot.A: The fibers cross **above** the cord, so a **left** tract lesion would weaken the **left** limbs, not his right
whyNot.B: The spinothalamic tract carries **pain and temperature**, which are **normal**; it cannot explain **spastic weakness**
whyNot.C: The fasciculus cuneatus carries **vibration and position sense**, not motor power, so it cannot cause **spastic weakness**
whyNot.D: A ventral horn lesion causes **flaccid weakness and low reflexes**; he is **stiff with brisk reflexes**, on the **right**

answer: Right lateral corticospinal tract in the cervical cord
why: **Spastic** weakness with **hyperreflexia and a Babinski sign** is an **upper motor neuron** lesion. The corticospinal fibers have already **crossed in the caudal medulla**, so a cord lesion causes weakness on the **same side**, the right.

idea.rule: In the cord the lateral corticospinal tract has already crossed, so damage causes same-side spastic weakness below the lesion.
also: Corticospinal fibers cross in the caudal medulla (pyramidal decussation)
Spinothalamic fibers cross within a segment or two of entry
Dorsal column fibers stay uncrossed until the medulla
Brown-Sequard: same-side weakness, opposite pain and temperature loss

stem: A 24-year-old man has a diving accident that dislocates the C6 vertebra on C7 and completely transects his spinal cord at that level.
oneliner: 24M + diving injury with C6 vertebral dislocation and complete cord transection → which movement is preserved?
ask: Which movement is most likely preserved?

whyNot.A: Elbow extension (triceps) is **C7**, which lies at the injury and is lost
whyNot.B: Finger abduction (interossei) is **C8-T1**, below the injury and lost
whyNot.D: Thumb abduction (abductor pollicis brevis) is **C8-T1**, below the injury and lost
whyNot.E: Finger flexion is mainly **C8**, below the injury and lost

why: In the neck each cord segment lies about **one vertebra higher than its number**, so the **C7 segment** sits at the **C6 vertebra**. A C6-on-C7 dislocation transects the cord at **C7**: everything from C7 down is lost, while **C5 and C6** survive, so **elbow flexion** (biceps) remains.

idea.rule: Cervical cord segments sit about one vertebra above their number, so a C6 vertebral injury damages the C7 segment and below.
also: Biceps and elbow flexion: C5-C6
Triceps and elbow extension: C7
Finger flexors and thumb abductors: C8-T1
Interossei and finger abduction: C8-T1

stem: A 22-year-old man falls from a motorcycle and fractures his clavicle. He cannot bend his elbow or turn his palm upward, his biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are reduced, and the skin over his lateral shoulder is numb.
oneliner: 22M + clavicle fracture, weak elbow flexion and supination, reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, numb lateral shoulder → which other movement is weak?
ask: Which other movement is most likely weak?

options.C: Bending the tip of the thumb
options.D: Raising the arm out to the side
options.E: Bending the fingers at the joints

whyNot.A: Elbow extension is **C7**, lower than the **C5-C6** pattern in his reflexes
whyNot.B: Finger abduction is **T1**, far below the injured roots
whyNot.C: Bending the thumb tip (flexor pollicis longus) is **C7-C8**, below the **C5-C6** pattern in his reflexes
whyNot.E: Finger flexion is mainly **C8**, below the **C5-C6** pattern in his reflexes

why: Weak elbow flexion and supination with reduced **biceps and brachioradialis reflexes** place the injury at the **upper trunk (C5-C6)**. It also takes **deltoid and supraspinatus**, so **shoulder abduction** is weak; elbow extension, hand and finger muscles are spared.

idea.rule: Upper trunk (C5-C6) injury weakens shoulder abduction, external rotation, elbow flexion and supination, sparing hand muscles.
also: Erb palsy is an upper trunk injury, with the arm adducted and medially rotated
Klumpke palsy (C8-T1) weakens the hand intrinsics
Supraspinatus starts shoulder abduction; the deltoid carries it to 90 degrees
The biceps reflex tests C5-C6

stem: A 9-year-old boy has tingling in his ring and little fingers after hanging from monkey bars by his arms. Sensation in his thumb and index finger is normal.
oneliner: 9M + tingling ring and little fingers after hanging from monkey bars, thumb and index sensation normal → which movement tests the nerve?
ask: Which movement best tests the motor function of the nerve involved?

options.B: Lifting the thumb away from the palm
options.C: Touching the thumb tip to the little finger
options.D: Straightening the fingers at the knuckles

whyNot.B: Thumb abduction uses the abductor pollicis brevis, supplied by the **median** nerve; his **thumb and index finger are normal**
whyNot.C: Opposition is a **median** nerve movement, and his **median-territory fingers are normal**
whyNot.D: Finger extension at the knuckles is a **radial** nerve movement; his tingling is in the **ring and little fingers**, ulnar skin
whyNot.E: Thumb extension is **radial**, and his tingling is in **ulnar** fingers

why: Tingling of the **ring and little fingers** with a normal thumb and index finger is an **ulnar** nerve stretch. The ulnar nerve (C8-T1) supplies the **interossei**, so **finger abduction** tests it.

idea.rule: The ulnar nerve supplies the interossei, so finger abduction and adduction test it.
also: Median nerve: thumb abduction and opposition
Radial nerve: extension of the wrist, fingers and thumb
Ulnar sensory loss affects the little finger and medial ring finger
Froment sign tests adductor pollicis (ulnar)

stem: A 30-year-old carpenter has hand numbness and tingling that wake him at night and ease when he shakes the hand. His thumb is weak when he lifts it away from the palm.
oneliner: 30M carpenter + night hand numbness and tingling relieved by shaking, weak thumb abduction → which skin area is numb?
ask: Which area of skin is most likely numb?

options.A: Dorsum of the hand and thumb at the first web space
options.B: Palmar little finger and medial half of ring finger
options.C: Lateral forearm and skin at the base of the thumb
options.D: Medial forearm and the medial half of the palm
options.E: Palmar thumb, index, middle and lateral ring fingers

whyNot.A: The back of the hand over the first web space is **radial**; his weak **thumb abduction** points to the median nerve
whyNot.B: The little and medial ring finger are **ulnar** skin, and the ulnar nerve does not supply the **thumb abductor** that is weak
whyNot.C: The lateral forearm is **musculocutaneous** skin, from a nerve that does not supply the **thumb abductor** that is weak
whyNot.D: The medial forearm and medial palm are **ulnar and medial cutaneous** skin, from nerves that do not supply the **thumb abductor** that is weak

answer: Palmar surface of the thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger (median nerve; carpal tunnel syndrome)
why: Night paresthesias relieved by shaking and **weak thumb abduction** (abductor pollicis brevis) are **carpal tunnel syndrome**. The compressed **median nerve** supplies the **palmar skin of the lateral three and a half fingers**.

idea.rule: Carpal tunnel compression of the median nerve numbs the palmar thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger.
also: Thenar skin is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel
Abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis weaken late
Phalen and Tinel signs reproduce the symptoms
Pregnancy, hypothyroidism and diabetes raise the risk

stem: A 41-year-old man used axillary crutches for 3 weeks after a severe ankle injury. He now has weak extension of the wrist and fingers, cannot raise his arm to the side well, and has numb skin over the lateral shoulder and back of the hand.
oneliner: 41M + 3 weeks axillary crutches, weak wrist and finger extension, weak arm abduction, numb lateral shoulder and dorsal hand → which part of the plexus?
ask: Which part of the brachial plexus is injured?

options.A: Radial nerve in the spiral groove

whyNot.A: A radial lesion in the spiral groove **spares the deltoid** and lateral shoulder skin; his **shoulder abduction is weak and numb**
whyNot.C: The lateral cord supplies **elbow flexors** and the median nerve; his weakness is in **extensors**
whyNot.D: The medial cord supplies **hand intrinsics** and medial skin; he has **dorsal hand and extensor** deficits
whyNot.E: An upper trunk (C5-C6) lesion spares the **finger extensors** (C7-C8), but his **finger extension is weak**

answer: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus (radial and axillary nerves)
why: The posterior cord gives the **radial** nerve (wrist and finger extensors) and the **axillary** nerve (deltoid and lateral shoulder skin). Axillary crutch pressure injures it, so **wrist extension and shoulder abduction** are both weak.

idea.rule: Radial plus axillary deficits together mean the posterior cord.
also: Posterior cord branches: upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary, radial
Radial nerve injury in the spiral groove causes wrist drop
Lateral cord: musculocutaneous and lateral root of median
Medial cord: ulnar and medial root of median

stem: A 35-year-old woman is struck by a car and has a fracture of the neck of her fibula. She cannot lift her foot, which slaps down as she walks, and the top of her foot is numb.
oneliner: 35F + car injury with fibular neck fracture, foot drop, numb top of foot → which exam pattern?
ask: Which examination pattern is most likely?

options.A: Weak plantar flexion and absent ankle jerk; dorsiflexion intact
options.B: Weak dorsiflexion and plantar flexion; eversion and ankle jerk intact
options.C: Weak dorsiflexion and eversion; plantar flexion, ankle jerk intact
options.D: Normal dorsiflexion and eversion; numbness over the sole
options.E: Weak eversion alone; dorsiflexion and plantar flexion intact

whyNot.A: Plantar flexion and the ankle jerk are **tibial**, a nerve that does not wind round the fibular neck; she has **foot drop**, not loss of push-off
whyNot.B: Plantar flexion is **tibial** and spared; her injury is **lateral** at the fibular neck
whyNot.D: She has **foot drop**, so dorsiflexion is lost, and the **sole** is tibial territory while her numbness is on the **dorsum**
whyNot.E: Her **foot drop** shows the deep branch is injured too, so dorsiflexion is lost along with eversion

answer: Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with preserved plantar flexion and ankle jerk (common fibular nerve injury)
why: The **common fibular nerve** winds around the **fibular neck**. Its deep branch lifts the foot (**dorsiflexion**) and its superficial branch **everts** it, with numbness of the **dorsum**. The **tibial nerve** keeps **plantar flexion and the Achilles reflex**.

idea.rule: Common fibular nerve injury weakens dorsiflexion and eversion but spares plantar flexion and the ankle jerk.
also: Deep fibular branch: dorsiflexion and web-space sensation
Superficial fibular branch: eversion and dorsal foot sensation
Tibial nerve: plantar flexion, inversion and the sole
Steppage gait results from foot drop
